extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/practitioners reviewing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and construing functional claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) and § 112(b), including identifying functional language, applying the three-prong test for § 112(f), determining the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI), assessing definiteness, and deciding appropriate rejections under compact prosecution principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Functional Language
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims often use functional language to add further description to some structure or action, for example how elements or steps tie together, or to provide context to claim elements. Functional language can appear in limitations that invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) ('means-plus-function'), and in limitations that do not invoke § 112(f). Limitations that do not invoke § 112(f) are typically recited with some structure, material or action to define a particular capability or purpose served by the recited structure, material or action. For more information, refer to MPEP 2111 and 2181 and specified training modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong analysis for invoking § 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the three-prong analysis in MPEP 2181 to determine whether the claim limitation invokes § 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prong A: does the limitation recite 'means' or a generic placeholder for 'means'? Prong B: is the generic placeholder modified by functional language? Prong C: is the limitation further modified by sufficient structure, material or acts for performing the claimed function? (If Prong A/B/C as applicable are met, § 112(f) may be invoked.) See MPEP 2181 and related training modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI of functional language when § 112(f) is invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: When § 112(f) is invoked, the BRI of the 'means-plus-function' limitation is restricted to the corresponding structure in the supporting disclosure, and its equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corresponding specification that identifies and links the structure, material or act to the function recited in the claim is considered to be part of the claim limitation. Example (Claim 5): corresponding structure may be aesthetic correction circuitry, or software and microprocessor with the disclosed algorithm (VMA = VA+VADA), and equivalents thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI of functional language when § 112(f) is not invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: When § 112(f) is not invoked and an element is recited along with a function, that element is construed as being capable of performing the function — i.e., the BRI of that element is limited by the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Claim 3): the recited elements of the system as a whole (scanner, aesthetic correction circuitry, display, disk memory) work together to perform the function; the BRI may be an intended use of the system. Example (Claim 4): the structure is the 'circuitry' and the BRI is that the circuitry has a structure that produces modified appearance signals based on user input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish recited function from intended use/result
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between reciting a function compared to reciting an intended use or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functional limitation can provide a patentable distinction (limit claim scope) by imposing limits on the function of a structure, material or action. Typically no patentable distinction (no limit on claim scope) is made by an intended use or result unless some structural difference is imposed by the use or result on the structure or material recited in the claim, or some manipulative difference is imposed by the use or result on the action recited in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the functional language limit claim scope (anticipation relevance)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the functional language limits the claim scope such that a prior art reference must disclose the functional limitation to anticipate the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If functional language modifies the structure recited in the claim (e.g., describes what the circuitry does and how), it can impose limits on the structure and thus must be shown by prior art to anticipate. If the functional language is merely an intended use that does not recite structure or provide context, it may not limit claim scope (prior art meeting structural limitations may anticipate regardless of explicit disclosure of the function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional limitations must have clearly defined boundaries to be definite under § 112(b); language that merely states a result without specifying ways to achieve it is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether one of ordinary skill in the art can determine what structure, material or act in the claim performs this function; whether the limitation has well defined boundaries or only expresses a problem solved or intended result; and what an anticipatory reference would need to disclose to satisfy this claim limitation. These considerations are not all-inclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for corresponding structure in 'means'-type § 112(f) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'means'-type claims, the specification must adequately disclose a corresponding structure or material that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate disclosure requires that the corresponding structure or material: (a) is disclosed so one of ordinary skill will understand what specific structure/material the inventor identified to perform the function; (b) is sufficient to perform the entire function recited in the claim limitation; and (c) is clearly linked to the function in the written description. See MPEP references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner action when claim boundaries are not reasonably clear
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner determines that the boundaries of a claim are not reasonably clear, a rejection under § 112(b) should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a rejection puts the applicant on notice to fulfill their statutory duty under § 112(b). In making a rejection, the examiner must identify the specific claim language that is indefinite and explain why it renders the boundaries unclear. When possible, the examiner should suggest how the indefiniteness issues may be resolved. Consider also other applicable rejections (e.g., §§ 101, 102, 103, and/or 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Part IV §112(f) factual checklist (disclosed structure / sufficiency / linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the functional language is part of a 'means'-type § 112(f) limitation, answer whether (A) specification discloses a structure/material performing the claimed function, (B) the disclosed structure/material is sufficient to perform the entire claimed function, and (C) the specification clearly links the structure/material to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each question, state Yes/No and provide the corresponding structure/material and explanatory notes. If any are negative, that supports indefiniteness or §112 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing boundaries for non-§112(f) functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: For functional language that does not invoke § 112(f), determine whether the boundaries of the functional language are clear such that one of ordinary skill in the art can draw the boundary between what is covered and what is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If boundaries are clear (e.g., which part of system modifies the signal, what the part does, and how signals have been modified), then do not reject under § 112(b). If boundaries are unclear, consider § 112(b) and suggest fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of indefinite functional language (§ 112(a) and prior art implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefinite, unbounded functional limitations typically lack an adequate written description under § 112(a) and may cover all ways of performing a function, indicating insufficient disclosure of possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, a § 112(b) rejection based on unclear functional boundaries should often be accompanied by a § 112(a) written description rejection. Additionally, because functional claim language not limited to specific structure can cover all devices/materials capable of performing the function, §§ 102 or 103 rejections may be appropriate if prior art discloses a device/material that can inherently perform the claimed function. When making prior art rejections, the examiner must state how the functional term is being interpreted with respect to the prior art applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution principle — examine all statutory requirements initially
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should, under compact prosecution principles, examine each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner determines that a claim term or phrase renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a § 112(b) rejection as well as any other applicable rejections (e.g., §§ 101, 102, 103, and/or 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art rejection considerations for functional/structural scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art X meets the structural elements recited in the claim, consider whether X explicitly discloses the recited function, or whether the structure in X performs the function with the same means, an equivalent means, or a different means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If functional language does not further limit the claim (structure recited does the work), then prior art meeting the structural limitations anticipates regardless of explicit disclosure of the function. If X is silent as to function, it cannot anticipate unless the function is inherent in X's disclosed structure (e.g., a commercial circuit whose manual indicates programming to perform the claimed function). If §112(f) limits the claim, a reference must disclose the corresponding structure or equivalent to anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a separate worksheet per claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim must be examined individually based on the particular elements recited therein; use a separate worksheet to analyze each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This worksheet is optional during examination but aids analysis and record clarity. The answer key includes example analyses and references to MPEP and training modules so examiners can obtain more information if needed.
